Commands, flags, environment variables, and default paths on this page were checked against the official documentation and source code as of Ollama v0.40.11 (released October 24, 2026): CLI Reference, FAQ, Context length, and API. Defaults can change between versions, so trust the output of ollama -v and ollama serve --help on your machine.
Install Ollama BASH Copy # Install on Linux; re-run the same script to upgrade curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh # Show the version ollama -v # Start the server manually (listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default) ollama serve On macOS and Windows, install the app from ollama.com/download. It downloads updates automatically; click “Restart to update” in the menu bar or taskbar to apply them. The Linux install script creates an ollama systemd service, so you usually do not need to run ollama serve yourself. Ollama command reference Command Purpose ollama pull MODEL Download or update a model ollama run MODEL [PROMPT] Run a model; pulls it first if it is not available locally ollama list / ollama ls List downloaded models ollama ps List models currently loaded in memory ollama show MODEL Show model information ollama stop MODEL Unload a model from memory immediately ollama cp SOURCE DESTINATION Copy a model under a new name ollama rm MODEL [MODEL...] Delete models (irreversible) ollama create NAME -f Modelfile Create a custom model from a Modelfile ollama serve Start the Ollama server BASH Copy # Download a model ollama pull llama3.2 # Interactive chat; type /bye to exit ollama run llama3.2 # One-shot prompt, handy in scripts ollama run llama3.2 "Explain RAG in three sentences." # Show timings and token speed ollama run llama3.2 --verbose # Control how long the model stays in memory ollama run llama3.2 --keepalive 30m # List downloaded models (ls is an alias of list) ollama list ollama ls # Show loaded models, their size, and GPU/CPU split ollama ps # Unload a model to free RAM / VRAM (files stay on disk) ollama stop llama3.2 In the PROCESSOR column of ollama ps, 100% GPU means the model is fully on the GPU, 100% CPU means it is fully in system memory, and 48%/52% CPU/GPU means it is split across both.
Inspect a model:
BASH Copy ollama show llama3.2 ollama show llama3.2 --modelfile # Modelfile ollama show llama3.2 --parameters # parameters ollama show llama3.2 --template # template ollama show llama3.2 --system # system message ollama show llama3.2 --license # license Use explicit model names and tags in scripts so that a change to a default model or latest does not silently alter results.
Delete models and free disk space ⚠️ Destructive: ollama rm deletes local models immediately, without a confirmation prompt, and cannot be undone. You must ollama pull the model again to use it.
BASH Copy # Check model names and sizes first ollama list # Delete one model ollama rm llama3.2 # Delete several models at once ollama rm llama3.2 mymodel Default model locations:
Platform Path macOS ~/.ollama/models Linux (official install script) /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models Windows C:\Users\%username%\.ollama\models If OLLAMA_MODELS is set, models are stored in that directory instead.
BASH Copy # Disk usage of the model directory (macOS) du -sh ~/.ollama/models # Linux (official install script) sudo du -sh /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models Prefer ollama rm over deleting individual files under blobs or manifests, which can leave model data inconsistent. By default the server prunes unused model blobs on startup; set OLLAMA_NOPRUNE=1 to disable this. ⚠️ Running rm -rf on the whole data directory (for example ~/.ollama on macOS or /usr/share/ollama on Linux) removes every model at once. The official docs only list this as an uninstall step; double-check the path first. If you only need to free memory rather than disk space, ollama stop MODEL is enough. Create a custom model with a Modelfile TEXT Copy # Modelfile FROM llama3.2 PARAMETER temperature 0.7 PARAMETER num_ctx 8192 SYSTEM You are a concise technical assistant. BASH Copy # Create the model (-f defaults to Modelfile in the current directory) ollama create my-assistant -f ./Modelfile # Run the custom model ollama run my-assistant # Copy a model before changing it so the original stays intact ollama cp my-assistant my-assistant-v2 Ollama settings: common environment variables The Ollama server is configured through environment variables. Run ollama serve --help for the full list.
Variable Purpose Default OLLAMA_HOST Server bind address and port 127.0.0.1:11434 OLLAMA_MODELS Model storage directory See “Default model locations” above OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE How long an idle model stays in memory; negative keeps it loaded, 0 unloads immediately 5m OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH Default context length Based on VRAM: 4k below 24 GiB, 32k for 24–48 GiB, 256k at 48 GiB or more OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL Parallel requests per model 1 OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS Models that can be loaded concurrently 3 × number of GPUs, or 3 for CPU inference OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE Requests queued while busy before returning 503 512 OLLAMA_ORIGINS Additional allowed CORS origins, comma-separated 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 allowed OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION 1 forces Flash Attention on, 0 disables it Automatic when supported OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE K/V cache quantization: f16, q8_0, q4_0 f16 OLLAMA_DEBUG Extra debug output, e.g. OLLAMA_DEBUG=1 Off OLLAMA_NOPRUNE Do not prune unused model blobs on startup Off OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD Disable cloud features such as cloud models and web search Off The FAQ still states a 4096-token default context length; check ollama serve --help for the default in your installed version. Raising OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL increases memory use in proportion to parallel requests × context length. The keep_alive parameter in an API request overrides OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE. Temporary setting (running ollama serve in the foreground):
BASH Copy OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434 OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=8192 ollama serve Set environment variables on macOS When Ollama runs as the macOS app, set variables with launchctl, then restart the app:
BASH Copy launchctl setenv OLLAMA_MODELS "/Volumes/Data/ollama/models" launchctl setenv OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE "30m" # Quit and reopen the Ollama app afterwards Set environment variables on Linux (systemd override) When Ollama runs as a systemd service, use an override instead of editing the installed unit file:
BASH Copy sudo systemctl edit ollama.service In the editor, add lines under [Service]:
INI Copy [Service] Environment="OLLAMA_MODELS=/data/ollama/models" Environment="OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m" Environment="OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2" BASH Copy # A custom model directory must be readable and writable by the ollama user sudo chown -R ollama:ollama /data/ollama/models # Reload and restart the service sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart ollama # View logs journalctl -e -u ollama Set environment variables on Windows Ollama on Windows inherits your user and system environment variables:
Quit Ollama from the taskbar. Open Settings (Windows 11) or Control Panel (Windows 10) and search for “environment variables”. Click “Edit environment variables for your account”. Create or edit user variables such as OLLAMA_HOST and OLLAMA_MODELS. Click OK/Apply to save. Start Ollama again from the Start menu. Pointing OLLAMA_MODELS at another drive keeps models from filling the system drive. If you change the model location, the uninstaller does not remove models stored there.
Exposing Ollama on your network BASH Copy # Listen on all interfaces (set it per platform as shown above) OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 ⚠️ The local API requires no authentication by default. With 0.0.0.0, anyone on the same network can run, pull, or delete models. Restrict access with a firewall, reverse proxy, or VPN, and do not expose it directly to the internet.
To let browser extensions call the API, allow their origins explicitly:
BASH Copy OLLAMA_ORIGINS=chrome-extension://*,moz-extension://*,safari-web-extension://* ollama serve REST API examples The local API base URL is http://localhost:11434/api; an OpenAI-compatible API is available at http://localhost:11434/v1.
BASH Copy # Server version curl http://localhost:11434/api/version # List downloaded models (same as ollama list) curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags # List loaded models (same as ollama ps) curl http://localhost:11434/api/ps # One-shot generation curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{ "model": "llama3.2", "prompt": "Describe Ollama in one sentence.", "stream": false }' # Chat with an explicit context length curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{ "model": "llama3.2", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Why is the sky blue?"}], "stream": false, "options": {"num_ctx": 8192} }' # Preload a model and keep it in memory curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{"model": "llama3.2", "keep_alive": -1}' # Unload a model immediately curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{"model": "llama3.2", "keep_alive": 0}' # ⚠️ Delete a model (same as ollama rm, irreversible) curl -X DELETE http://localhost:11434/api/delete -d '{"model": "llama3.2"}' Python example:
PYTHON Copy import requests def chat_with_ollama(prompt, model="llama3.2"): response = requests.post( "http://localhost:11434/api/chat", json={ "model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], "stream": False, }, timeout=120, ) response.raise_for_status() return response.json()["message"]["content"] print(chat_with_ollama("Summarize the following text in three bullet points: ...")) The local API is useful for private experiments; production systems still need timeouts, retries, and logging.

Docker basics Image management:
BASH Copy # Search for images docker search nginx docker search ubuntu # Pull images docker pull nginx docker pull nginx:alpine docker pull ubuntu:24.04 # List images docker images docker image ls # Remove images docker rmi nginx docker rmi nginx:alpine docker image rm ubuntu:24.04 # Clean up unused images docker image prune # Remove dangling images docker image prune -a # Remove all images not used by any container Container operations Running containers:
BASH Copy # Basic run docker run nginx docker run -d nginx # Run in the background (detached) docker run -it ubuntu bash # Interactive mode docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash # Remove the container automatically on exit # Port mapping docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx # Map host port 8080 to container port 80 docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx # Bind to localhost only # Bind-mount directories docker run -d -v /host/path:/container/path nginx docker run -d -v $(pwd):/app node # Mount the current directory # Environment variables docker run -d -e ENV_VAR=value nginx docker run -d --env-file .env nginx # Name the container docker run -d --name my-nginx nginx Managing containers:
BASH Copy # List containers docker ps # Running containers docker ps -a # All containers docker container ls # Stop containers docker stop container_id docker stop my-nginx docker kill container_id # Force stop # Start a stopped container docker start container_id docker restart container_id # Remove containers docker rm container_id docker rm my-nginx docker rm -f container_id # Force-remove a running container # Clean up stopped containers docker container prune Name long-running containers so logs and operational commands are easier to read.
Interacting with and debugging containers BASH Copy # Open a shell in a running container docker exec -it container_id bash docker exec -it my-nginx sh # View container logs docker logs container_id docker logs -f container_id # Follow logs in real time docker logs --tail 100 container_id # Show the last 100 lines # Inspect containers docker inspect container_id docker stats container_id # Live resource usage docker top container_id # Processes inside the container # Copy files docker cp file.txt container_id:/path/ # Copy into the container docker cp container_id:/path/file.txt . # Copy out of the container # Show filesystem changes in the container docker diff container_id Docker Compose Basic commands:
BASH Copy # Start services docker compose up docker compose up -d # Run in the background docker compose up --build # Rebuild images # Stop services docker compose down docker compose down -v # Also remove volumes docker compose stop # Check service status docker compose ps docker compose logs docker compose logs -f service_name # Follow logs for one service # Run commands docker compose exec service_name bash docker compose run service_name command # Restart services docker compose restart docker compose restart service_name Use down -v only when the volume data is disposable.
Example docker-compose.yml:
YAML Copy services: web: image: nginx:latest ports: - "8080:80" volumes: - ./html:/usr/share/nginx/html db: image: mysql:8.4 environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: password MYSQL_DATABASE: myapp volumes: - db_data:/var/lib/mysql volumes: db_data: Building images (Dockerfile) Basic Dockerfile:
DOCKERFILE Copy # Node.js application example FROM node:24-alpine WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 USER node CMD ["npm", "start"] Build commands:
BASH Copy # Build an image docker build -t my-app . docker build -t my-app:v1.0 . docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t my-app:prod . # Multi-stage build docker build --target production -t my-app:prod . # Pass build arguments docker build --build-arg NODE_ENV=production -t my-app . # Show image build history docker history my-app Docker networking BASH Copy # List networks docker network ls # Create networks docker network create my-network docker network create --driver bridge my-bridge # Connect a container to a network docker network connect my-network container_id # Disconnect a container from a network docker network disconnect my-network container_id # Inspect a network docker network inspect my-network # Remove a network docker network rm my-network # Clean up unused networks docker network prune Docker volumes BASH Copy # List volumes docker volume ls # Create a volume docker volume create my-volume # Inspect a volume docker volume inspect my-volume # Use a volume docker run -d -v my-volume:/data nginx # Remove a volume docker volume rm my-volume # Clean up unused anonymous volumes (Docker 23+ needs -a to include named volumes) docker volume prune # Back up a volume docker run --rm -v my-volume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup ubuntu tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data . # Restore a volume docker run --rm -v my-volume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup ubuntu tar xzf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data Docker system cleanup BASH Copy # Show Docker disk usage docker system df # Clean up unused resources docker system prune # Stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and build cache docker system prune -a # Also unused images docker system prune -a --volumes # Also unused anonymous volumes # Clean up by resource type docker container prune # Stopped containers docker image prune # Dangling images docker image prune -a # All unused images docker network prune # Unused networks docker volume prune # Unused anonymous volumes # Force-remove all containers docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq) # Remove all images docker rmi -f $(docker images -q) Check disk usage before pruning shared build hosts.
Docker registry BASH Copy # Log in to a registry docker login docker login registry.example.com echo "$REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u username --password-stdin registry.example.com # Keeps the password out of shell history and the process list # Tag images docker tag my-app:latest registry.example.com/my-app:latest docker tag my-app:latest harbor.company.com/project/my-app:v1.0 # Push images docker push registry.example.com/my-app:latest docker push harbor.company.com/project/my-app:v1.0 # Pull from a private registry docker pull harbor.company.com/project/my-app:v1.0 # Log out docker logout docker logout registry.example.com

Checked against the official GitLab documentation on October 26, 2026, when the latest GitLab Runner release was v19.5.1. Settings and defaults change between versions; before production use, check Runner advanced configuration, Registering runners, and Predefined CI/CD variables.
privileged = true, mounting /var/run/docker.sock, gitlab-runner unregister, and gitlab-runner verify --delete carry security or irreversible risks and are flagged below. Back up config.toml before changing it. Runner tokens and registry passwords are secrets; keep them out of repositories and CI logs.
Register a runner (authentication token workflow) The current workflow creates the runner in GitLab first, then registers it with a runner authentication token:
For a project runner, go to Settings > CI/CD > Runners and select Create project runner (Maintainer role required). Group and instance runners are created from group settings or the Admin Area. Set tags and a description, then create the runner. GitLab shows an authentication token starting with glrt- only briefly. Register on the runner host: BASH Copy sudo gitlab-runner register \ --non-interactive \ --url "https://gitlab.example.com/" \ --token "$RUNNER_TOKEN" \ --executor "docker" \ --docker-image alpine:latest \ --docker-pull-policy "if-not-present" \ --description "docker-runner" Legacy registration tokens (--registration-token) are deprecated and, according to the docs, scheduled for removal in GitLab 20.0. Use authentication tokens for every new runner. Tags, protected status, and run-untagged are set when the runner is created in the GitLab UI or API, not through register arguments. To automate runner creation, call POST /api/v4/user/runners with an access token that has the create_runner scope, then pass the returned token to register: BASH Copy curl --silent --request POST --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/user/runners" \ --data "runner_type=project_type" \ --data "project_id=<project_id>" \ --data "description=docker-runner" \ --data "tag_list=docker,linux" \ --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <project_access_token>" About gitlab_pat: config.toml has no gitlab_pat setting. The runner authenticates with the token under [[runners]] (the glrt- runner authentication token). A personal access token (glpat- prefix) is only for API automation such as creating runners; it does not belong in config.toml.
config.toml location Install type config.toml path Linux/macOS run as root (sudo) /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml Linux/macOS run as a regular user ~/.gitlab-runner/config.toml Windows The install folder, for example C:\GitLab-Runner\config.toml Other systems ./config.toml in the current directory Docker container /etc/gitlab-runner/ inside the container, usually mounted from /srv/gitlab-runner/config on the host or a Docker volume Docker container install, as shown in the official docs:
BASH Copy docker run -d --name gitlab-runner --restart always \ -v /srv/gitlab-runner/config:/etc/gitlab-runner \ -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \ gitlab/gitlab-runner:latest This hands the host Docker socket to the runner container; see the risks under “Docker-in-Docker vs socket binding”.
Reloading: the runner checks config.toml every 3 seconds and reloads changes automatically, or on SIGHUP. Most settings need no restart; listen_address is the exception.
Common config.toml settings TOML Copy concurrent = 4 # max concurrent jobs across all runners; 0 is not allowed check_interval = 3 # seconds between job requests to GitLab; default 3 log_level = "info" # debug / info / warn / error / fatal / panic shutdown_timeout = 30 # seconds before forced shutdown; default 30 [[runners]] name = "docker-runner" # informational only url = "https://gitlab.example.com/" token = "glrt-REDACTED" # authentication token, not the registration token executor = "docker" # shell, docker, kubernetes, ... limit = 0 # max concurrent jobs for this runner; 0 means no limit request_concurrency = 1 # concurrent job requests to GitLab; default 1 environment = ["TZ=Asia/Taipei"] # append or override job environment variables [runners.docker] image = "alpine:latest" # used when a job does not set an image privileged = false # disables container isolation when true; see below volumes = ["/cache"] # extra mounts, docker -v syntax pull_policy = "if-not-present" # never / if-not-present / always; default always allowed_images = ["registry.example.com/*"] # restrict job images; unset allows all shm_size = 0 [runners.cache] Type = "s3" # s3 / gcs / azure Path = "runner-cache" # prepended to the cache URL Shared = true # share cache between runners; default false [runners.cache.s3] ServerAddress = "s3.example.com" BucketName = "gitlab-runner-cache" BucketLocation = "ap-northeast-1" AuthenticationType = "iam" # iam or access-key concurrent caps the whole runner process; limit caps one [[runners]] entry. Both apply. pull_policy = "if-not-present" speeds up job start, but stale images already on the host are not refreshed; pin tags or digests. In [runners.cache.s3], AuthenticationType defaults to access-key when ServerAddress, AccessKey, and SecretKey are all set, otherwise iam. AccessKey and SecretKey are secrets; prefer an IAM role. listen_address = ":9252" enables Prometheus metrics; without it, metrics are off. Changing it requires a restart. Docker-in-Docker vs socket binding There are two common ways to run docker build inside a job:
Approach Settings Benefit Risk Docker-in-Docker (DinD) privileged = true, volumes = ["/certs/client", "/cache"] Each job gets its own Docker daemon, so jobs do not conflict Privileged mode effectively disables container security mechanisms and can allow escape to the host Docker socket binding volumes = ["/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock", "/cache"], privileged = false No privileged mode; shares the host image cache Hands the host Docker daemon to jobs: container breakout, privilege escalation, or deleting the runner’s own containers Security warning: both privileged = true and a mounted docker.sock give jobs close to root access on the host. Enable them only on dedicated runners for trusted projects, never on shared runners that run forks or untrusted code.
.gitlab-ci.yml for DinD with TLS:
YAML Copy build-image: image: docker:<version>-cli # use a version your team has validated services: - docker:<version>-dind variables: DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs" script: - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" . Socket binding limitations: it cannot be combined with the docker:dind service, volume paths in jobs resolve against the host, and containers with fixed names conflict between concurrent jobs.
Private registries such as Harbor When the runner pulls job or service images from a private registry such as Harbor, provide credentials with DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG:
BASH Copy # Build the auth value; printf avoids encoding a trailing newline printf "my_username:my_password" | openssl base64 -A JSON Copy { "auths": { "harbor.example.com": { "auth": "<base64 of username:password>" } } } Set it as a project or group CI/CD variable named DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG (masked is recommended), in [[runners]] environment (escape the double quotes), or in .docker/config.json on the runner host. Lookup order: /root/.docker/config.json → CI/CD variable → environment in config.toml → $HOME/.docker/config.json of the user running the runner. The auths key must match the image reference exactly; for harbor.example.com:5000/..., the key must be harbor.example.com:5000. Prefer a Harbor robot account scoped to the projects it needs. To push to the built-in GitLab Container Registry, use the predefined variables:
YAML Copy script: - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login "$CI_REGISTRY" -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD equals CI_JOB_TOKEN and expires when the job ends; use a deploy token for long-lived access. Pushing to Harbor requires your own masked CI/CD variables holding robot account credentials.
Useful gitlab-runner commands BASH Copy sudo gitlab-runner list # list runners in config.toml sudo gitlab-runner verify # check registered runners can reach GitLab sudo gitlab-runner status # service status; exit code 0 when running sudo gitlab-runner restart # stop, then start the service sudo gitlab-runner start sudo gitlab-runner stop # Reload config.toml without a restart sudo kill -SIGHUP <main_runner_pid> Irreversible commands (back up config.toml first):
BASH Copy # Remove runners that no longer exist in GitLab; rewrites config.toml sudo gitlab-runner verify --delete # Unregister by name; with duplicate names only the first is removed sudo gitlab-runner unregister --name docker-runner # Unregister by URL and token sudo gitlab-runner unregister --url "https://gitlab.example.com/" --token "$RUNNER_TOKEN" # Unregister every runner sudo gitlab-runner unregister --all-runners For runners created in the GitLab UI or API, unregister removes only the runner manager; delete the runner in the UI or through the API to remove it completely. Without sudo, the runner runs in user mode and uses ~/.gitlab-runner/config.toml, a common cause of “runner not found”. Do not use killall or pkill on runners with the shell or docker executor; it can break signal handling. Send SIGQUIT for a graceful stop. Common predefined CI/CD variables Variable Value Notes CI_COMMIT_SHA Full commit hash the pipeline builds CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA First 8 characters of CI_COMMIT_SHA Common image tag CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME Branch or tag name being built CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME lowercased, non-alphanumerics replaced with -, max 63 bytes Safe for URLs, hostnames, image tags CI_COMMIT_BRANCH Branch name Not available in merge request or tag pipelines CI_COMMIT_TAG Tag name Only in tag pipelines CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH Project default branch name CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE How the pipeline was triggered For example push, merge_request_event, schedule, web, api, trigger, parent_pipeline CI_PIPELINE_ID Pipeline ID, unique across the instance Job-only CI_JOB_ID Job ID, unique across the instance Job-only CI_REGISTRY Container Registry address (<host>[:<port>]) Only when the registry is enabled for the instance CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE Base image path for the project (<host>[:<port>]/<project_full_path>) Only when the registry is enabled for the project CI_REGISTRY_USER / CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD Credentials for pushing to the project registry Password equals CI_JOB_TOKEN and expires with the job CI_PROJECT_DIR Full path where the repository is cloned and the job runs Follows builds_dir when set CI_PROJECT_NAME / CI_PROJECT_PATH Project directory name / namespace plus project name CI_JOB_TOKEN Token for certain API endpoints Valid only while the job runs; never print it CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME Job environment name Only when environment:name is set CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID Merge request ID within the project Only in merge request pipelines CI_SERVER_URL Base GitLab instance URL, including protocol and port GITLAB_USER_LOGIN Username of the user who started the pipeline For manual jobs, the user who started the job A common pattern for pipeline-type rules:
YAML Copy deploy: script: - echo "Deploy $CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA to $CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME" environment: name: production rules: - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule" # skip scheduled pipelines when: never - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG # deploy only from tag pipelines Further reading: for full .gitlab-ci.yml, Harbor, and multi-environment deployment examples, see the GitLab CI/CD guide.

Since 2022, I have been bringing LLMs into real product workflows. One part of that work is an internal text summarization and AI application platform that integrates the OpenAI API, Ollama, local models, and batch processing, with the focus on model usage that stays controllable and maintainable.
The details of an internal system like this are not suitable for publication, so this is not a full case study. Instead, it collects the principles and trade-offs I apply when designing and operating a summarization pipeline. API behavior described here was checked against the official documentation at the time of writing (October 2026); check the latest docs before relying on it.
Why summarization is more than an API call A summarization demo is quick to build: put the text in a prompt, ask the model to summarize it, and you have a result in minutes. The real work starts after the demo:
Input length varies, and some texts exceed the model’s context length. A batch contains many items, so you run into rate limits, timeouts, and partial failures. Downstream systems need a fixed format, but model output is not always shaped the same way. Cost, latency, and data sensitivity all affect which model each item should go to. After changing a model or a prompt, you need to know whether quality improved or regressed. That is why I design summarization as a data processing pipeline rather than a single API call.
Breaking down the pipeline I split the flow into stages that can each be observed and re-run on their own:
Preprocessing: remove formatting noise, duplicated content, and fields the model does not need, and handle data that should not leave the environment at this step. Cleaner input makes both token usage and output quality easier to control. Chunking: estimate the token count first. If the text exceeds what the model can handle, split it on paragraph or semantic boundaries, with a small overlap where needed so key points are not cut in half. Model calls: summarize short texts directly. For long texts, use a map-reduce approach: summarize each chunk, then combine the chunk summaries into a final summary. Every call stays within a controlled input size, and a failure only requires re-running one chunk. Validation: check output format, required fields, length, and obvious errors. Anything that fails is marked as failed or sent to retry. Output: store the result together with the model used, the prompt version, and the processing status, so it can be traced and compared later. With local models, pay close attention to context length. Ollama picks its default context length based on available VRAM; you can change it with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH and confirm the actual allocation in the CONTEXT column of ollama ps (Context length docs). If you do not check this setting, the model may not see all of a long text. I keep Ollama installation, commands, and environment variables in Ollama Commands and Settings.
Structured output for downstream systems When summaries are consumed by other systems, I ask the model for JSON and constrain the fields with a schema:
OpenAI Structured Outputs in strict mode makes the output follow a supplied JSON Schema. JSON mode only guarantees valid JSON, not schema adherence. You still need to handle refusals and responses that are incomplete because they hit the output token limit. Ollama supports JSON schemas through the format parameter, and through response_format on its OpenAI-compatible API. The docs recommend also including the schema in the prompt and setting temperature to 0 for more consistent results (Structured outputs docs). A schema only guarantees the shape, not the content. Output that passes format validation can still miss key points or include things that are not in the source.
Choosing between cloud APIs and local models In my post on Gemma 4 12B (in Traditional Chinese), I argued that the point of local models is not to replace cloud models but to fill in a deployable middle tier. That is also my starting point when choosing models for summarization:
Cloud APIs suit tasks that need stronger comprehension, longer context, or more complex instructions, and they spare you from maintaining GPUs and runtimes. Local models solve a different set of problems: whether the workload can run in a private environment, whether data can stay in your own environment, and whether inference cost and latency can be controlled. In practice I do not rely on only one. A better approach is to let both plug into the same pipeline. Ollama provides an OpenAI-compatible API (by default at http://localhost:11434/v1/ locally), so the same client code can switch by changing the base URL and model name (OpenAI compatibility docs). Compatible does not mean identical, though. For example, context length cannot be set through the OpenAI-compatible API, so test each backend before switching.
When choosing, I look at data sensitivity, required quality, acceptable latency, overall cost, and how a quantized model actually performs on the available hardware. Benchmarks are only a reference; in the end you have to test with your own data.
Batch processing, retries, and cost control Batch processing For work that does not need immediate results, I use batch processing. The OpenAI Batch API takes requests as a JSONL file, completes within 24 hours, costs 50% less than synchronous calls, and has its own rate limits. Output order may not match input order, so results must be matched back by each request’s custom_id. Failed and expired requests go to a separate error file that needs its own handling.
Local models have no hosted batch service like this, so you control the pace yourself: limit concurrency so you do not exhaust GPU memory or overload the service.
Retries Retries need rules; they cannot resend forever. The OpenAI rate limits guide recommends:
Wait according to Retry-After when it is present; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. Cap both the number of retries and the total wait time. Failed requests still count toward per-minute limits, so continuously resending makes recovery harder. The official SDKs retry some errors automatically, so avoid double-counting when you implement your own retries. Do not retry quota or billing errors. I add one more principle: retry per chunk or per item, and make sure you can tell which parts already succeeded, so you never have to re-run a whole batch.
Cost control Most of the cost is decided at design time:
Remove unnecessary content during preprocessing to cut input tokens. Set max_tokens close to the expected output length. OpenAI counts the larger of max_tokens and the estimated request tokens toward rate limits, so an oversized value wastes capacity. Send non-urgent work to the Batch API or to local models. Record the model and token usage for each call so you can see where the cost goes. Validating output quality Summary quality is hard to judge with automation alone, so I use two layers:
Automated checks: whether the schema passes, required fields exist, length is reasonable, and whether any output was refused or truncated. These are hard requirements; anything that fails does not move downstream. Human spot checks: regularly sample summaries and compare them with the source, looking for missed key points, distorted meaning, or content that is not in the source. Compare the same sample set before and after changing a model or prompt to know whether the change actually helped. The OpenAI docs also note that structured output only guarantees format, and that you should build evaluations to confirm the content meets your needs. Keep the spot-check samples and results so they can be reused the next time you change models.
What I learned Design the pipeline first, then pick the model. Once preprocessing, chunking, validation, and retries are in place, switching models becomes much cheaper. Cloud and local are not an either-or choice. Let both plug into the same pipeline, then decide per type of work based on data, quality, and cost. Correct format is not correct content. Schema validation catches format errors but not summaries that miss key points, so human spot checks cannot be skipped. Traceability matters more than getting it right the first time. Keep the model, prompt version, token usage, and processing status so you know where to start when something goes wrong.

Since 2023, I have planned and operated Proxmox VE, Proxmox Backup Server (PBS), GPU servers, and On-prem infrastructure as an operator. The environment runs internal services and AI runtime workloads, and I am responsible for the overall backup strategy.
This is not an installation guide. It summarizes the planning principles I care about in small and mid-sized on-prem environments, plus problems I actually ran into and documented on my blog (the linked posts are written in Traditional Chinese). It does not include hostnames, IP addresses, network layouts, or security details. Configuration advice here is general guidance, and the official Proxmox documentation remains the reference.
Background and Requirements On-prem requirements are usually practical: a set of internal services has to run reliably for a long time, AI workloads need GPUs, and data has to be backed up and restorable. Budget and headcount are limited, so the platform has to be maintainable by a small team.
Proxmox VE fits this situation well. VMs and LXC containers are managed in the same interface, clustering, storage, and backup have built-in approaches, and PBS adds incremental, deduplicated backups. For me, the point is not having the most features. It is whether we can investigate and recover quickly when something breaks.
My responsibilities in this area include:
Designing and operating Proxmox VE clusters, virtualization, storage, and the VM lifecycle. Building Proxmox Backup Server and planning backup, restore, and disaster recovery processes. Managing NVIDIA GPU servers, drivers and runtimes, inference environments, and system tuning. Evaluating Dell, HP, and Supermicro server hardware and GPU server specifications, and turning them into specs that can be purchased and operated. Planning internal and external data center paths, site-to-site backup, and high availability, and using LibreNMS for network and server monitoring. Planning: Cluster, Storage, and Network Cluster A cluster gives you central management and VM mobility, but it also brings quorum into the picture. According to the Proxmox VE documentation, High Availability needs at least three nodes for reliable quorum. A two-node cluster can use a QDevice as the third vote.
A few other things I check early:
Consistent node versions: the documentation recommends keeping all nodes on the same version, so upgrades should be planned and rolled out node by node. CPU compatibility: online migration is only guaranteed between CPUs from the same vendor. With mixed hardware, choose a conservative CPU model for VMs, or live migration may fail. Node lifecycle: adding, replacing, and removing nodes should follow a fixed procedure, not improvisation. Storage The principle is to separate things that grow from the system itself. VM disks, ISOs and templates, and backup data each have a suitable place. Backup data in particular should not share space with the hypervisor’s system disk, or a spike on one side will take down the other.
VM disks should also be expected to grow. Expanding a disk in Proxmox is easy, but after resizing on the hypervisor side, the partition, LVM, and filesystem inside the guest OS also need to be adjusted. I documented the full steps for an Ubuntu 22.04 VM on my blog.
Network Cluster communication uses Corosync, which is sensitive to latency but does not need much bandwidth. The documentation recommends a dedicated physical NIC for cluster traffic and a second link on a different physical network for redundancy, so VM or backup traffic cannot crowd out Corosync.
As a general principle, plan management, cluster, VM, and backup traffic separately, and settle the addressing plan at the start. Changing a cluster’s communication addresses later costs more than you might expect (see the operational issues below).
GPU Servers and AI Workloads AI runtimes are sensitive to GPU, driver, CUDA, and kernel versions. The operational goal for GPU servers is an environment that can be rebuilt, not a machine that happens to work.
A common way to use GPUs on Proxmox is PCI(e) passthrough. The documentation points out several trade-offs to think through first:
The hardware and BIOS / UEFI must support IOMMU, and it must be enabled. Once a GPU is passed through to a VM, the host and other VMs can no longer use that card. VMs with passed-through PCI devices currently cannot be live-migrated, so node maintenance needs planned downtime. Because of these limits, it helps to plan GPU workloads per machine: which services need exclusive GPU access, how drivers and runtimes are versioned, and how services are stopped and brought back during host maintenance.
Driver problems are the most common issue in GPU operations. I documented how I handled nvidia-smi reporting “No devices were found” and NVIDIA drivers failing to load under Secure Boot on Ubuntu 24.04. The common lesson: first understand how the kernel, driver, Secure Boot, and build environment relate to each other, then decide on a fix, instead of reinstalling repeatedly.
Proxmox Backup Server Backup Strategy I look at backup strategy as four parts: backup, retention, cleanup, and verification, plus restore drills on top.
Prune and Garbage Collection Are Different Things This is the most commonly misunderstood part of PBS. According to the PBS documentation:
Prune only removes snapshot metadata (manifests, indexes, and so on). The chunks that hold the actual data are not removed immediately. Garbage Collection (GC) is what actually deletes chunks no longer referenced by any snapshot. GC runs in two phases, mark and sweep, with a grace period (about 24 hours and 5 minutes by default), so running GC right after a prune does not necessarily free space immediately. Retention settings (keep-last, keep-daily, keep-weekly, and so on) and the GC schedule should be designed together. Pruning without scheduled GC lets usage keep growing. Scheduling GC with an overly generous retention policy runs out of space just the same.
Keep Headroom; Do Not Wait for 100% I documented how I handled a PBS disk that reached 100% usage. The trap was that GC needs some free space to run, but there was none left. The fix was to delete task logs older than 90 days to free a little space, then run GC manually.
That experience made me care more about a few things:
Monitor datastore usage and act while there is still headroom, not when writes start failing. Keep the datastore and the PBS system space as separate as possible so backup data cannot fill up the system. Regularly check that prune and GC jobs are actually running and not failing. Verification and Restore Drills A successful backup is not the same as a restorable one. The PBS documentation recommends verify jobs and re-verifying all backups at least monthly, because aging disks can slowly corrupt previously good backups (bit rot). A good pattern is a frequent verify job for new backups, plus a weekly or monthly full re-verification.
Beyond verification, real restore drills matter: periodically restore a few VMs or containers to a test environment and confirm they boot, services run, and the data is the expected version. Proxmox VE also offers live-restore and single file restore, which are worth exercising during drills.
Off-site Copies and Disaster Recovery A single backup copy in the same data center is not enough if the whole site has a problem. PBS can use remotes and sync jobs to replicate backups to another PBS, which forms the basis of site-to-site backup. The key is to also document how and where backups at the other site would be restored, as part of the disaster recovery process, rather than just having the data sitting there.
Operational Issues I Ran Into Each item below is a problem I documented publicly on my blog. Here I only summarize the key points and what I learned.
Changing the Cluster Communication IP I documented the process of updating Proxmox VE cluster IPs and syncing the configuration. The key is to edit the cluster-shared /etc/pve/corosync.conf, not /etc/corosync/corosync.conf on a single node. Back it up first, increment config_version when editing, update each node’s network settings and /etc/hosts, and confirm with pvecm status that the change has been applied. This affects quorum, so it is a high-risk change that belongs in a maintenance window.
Removing a Node from the Cluster For node replacement, I wrote up how to safely remove a node from a Proxmox VE cluster: back up or migrate the node’s VMs and containers, shut it down and make sure it will not power back on, remove it with pvecm delnode, and then clean up the leftover node directory and SSH key entries. The official documentation also stresses that a removed node must not rejoin the same cluster network with its old configuration, or the cluster may break.
NIC Firmware Errors I documented a Proxmox VE host where an Intel X550 kept logging ixgbe FWSM firmware errors. Packet counters looked normal and a kernel update did not help. The errors only went away after updating the NIC’s NVM and doing a real power cycle. The lesson: do not handle firmware warnings read from the hardware by filtering logs. Before flashing firmware, take an inventory, confirm version compatibility, and have BMC / IPMI or a physical console ready.
Repairing VMs and Containers A Windows VM that will not boot: I documented repairing a Windows VM on PVE with WinPE. WinPE may not include VirtIO drivers, so you need to load them with drvload before the system disk is visible, then repair with offline DISM. IPv6 in LXC: I documented that enabling IPv6 for LXC containers on PVE required adjusting the host’s accept_ra setting. Wrong Web UI certificate: I documented PVE showing Connection error 596 after an incorrect certificate was installed. The fix was to SSH in and replace the pveproxy certificate files with the correct ones. Older Hardware and Hardware Monitoring I documented a fix for striped display output when installing PVE or PBS on an HP ProLiant DL380 G6, and installing HPE Agentless Management on Proxmox so iLO can read the host status. Older hardware can stay in service longer, but expect installer and monitoring tool support to shrink over time, and plan replacements early.
Checks Before Upgrading I wrote about several important new features in Proxmox VE 9.2, such as HA disarm / arm, dynamic load balancing in CRS, and the Custom CPU Models GUI. Whatever the version, before upgrading production I confirm that backups are complete, kernel and driver compatibility is fine, HA and migration behave as expected, and network configuration is unaffected, and I validate on a test environment or non-critical node first.
What I Learned Backups should be judged by whether they restore: prune, GC, verification, and restore drills are all required. A successful backup job alone is not enough. Monitor space and capacity early: once PBS reaches 100%, even the cleanup tools struggle to run. Keeping headroom is far cheaper than firefighting. Cluster changes are high-risk operations: changing IPs, removing nodes, and upgrading all call for backing up configuration first, following the documented procedure, and scheduling a maintenance window. Write down the problems you hit: every issue above can be looked up in my own notes next time, which is why I keep writing on my blog.
summary:
Since 2023, I have planned and operated Proxmox VE, Proxmox Backup Server (PBS), GPU servers, and On-prem infrastructure as an operator. The environment runs internal services and AI runtime workloads, and I am responsible for the overall backup strategy.
This is not an installation guide. It summarizes the planning principles I care about in small and mid-sized on-prem environments, plus problems I actually ran into and documented on my blog (the linked posts are written in Traditional Chinese). It does not include hostnames, IP addresses, network layouts, or security details. Configuration advice here is general guidance, and the official Proxmox documentation remains the reference.

Since 2022, I have built and maintained self-hosted GitLab, GitLab Runner, Harbor registry, and CI/CD workflows as an Operator, connecting source code, container images, and deployment into one flow.
This is not a setup tutorial. Examples for .gitlab-ci.yml, Runner deployment, and multi-environment deployment are in the GitLab CI/CD Guide: Runner Setup, .gitlab-ci.yml, Harbor, and Deployments, and config.toml options and common variables are in GitLab Runner config.toml Configuration and Common CI/CD Variables. This post covers the other side: why you would run this stack yourself, how the components fit together, and where the time actually goes after a few years. Each problem mentioned below links to the record I wrote at the time on blog.clarence.tw.
Why Consider Self-hosting GitLab.com and the cloud registries are mature, so self-hosting is not the default answer. It usually comes from several considerations stacking up:
Where code and data live: some teams need source code, images, and build logs to stay in an environment they control. Network environment: when deployment targets are on-premises or on an internal network, keeping Runners and the registry on the same side shortens build and image pull paths and makes outbound traffic easier to control. Runner resources: jobs that need specific hardware, operating systems, or larger build capacity are easier to schedule on your own Runners. Integration: the platform has to connect with existing identity, monitoring, and backup processes. The cost is equally clear: upgrades, backups, certificates, signing keys, disk space, and troubleshooting all become your responsibility. Before self-hosting, make sure someone is willing to own that work for the long term.
The Overall Flow The flow fits in one sentence: code goes into GitLab, Runners build and test it according to the pipeline, the resulting container image is pushed to Harbor, and the deployment environment pulls the image from Harbor.
Source: a developer pushes a commit or tag to GitLab, which triggers a pipeline. CI: GitLab assigns jobs to Runners with matching tags, which run tests and build the image. Image: the built image is pushed to the matching Harbor project according to the tagging rules. Deploy: the deployment environment pulls a specific image version from Harbor with a pull-only account. Splitting it this way gives each stage a clear responsibility. When a pipeline fails, you can first decide whether the problem is in source, build, push, or deploy instead of guessing across the whole chain.
There is not always just one registry. In 2021 I wrote about using Jib and Gradle in GitLab CI to push images to GitLab Container Registry, Azure Container Registry, and Amazon ECR. The ECR login flow required me to build a separate image with the AWS CLI and a credential helper. Every additional registry adds another authentication method and another way for things to break.
Runner Strategy Runners are the part of CI/CD that gets adjusted most often. A few general principles help:
Route with tags: send different kinds of jobs (regular builds, jobs that need Docker, special environments) to different Runners so they do not compete for resources. Minimize privileges: privileged mode and mounting the Docker socket effectively hand host access to the job. Enable them only for projects that need them and can be trusted. Treat the config as an asset: config.toml contains runner tokens. Back it up before editing and never commit it to a repository. Runner versions and helper images can break too. In 2020, on the docker-windows executor, I ran into Missing gitlab-runner-helper errors that disabled artifact uploads, and fixed it by setting helper_image in config.toml. See the Runner note linked above for specific options and their risks.
Harbor and Image Management Robot Accounts and CI Authentication When CI pushes images to Harbor, I use a Harbor robot account rather than a personal account. According to the Harbor documentation, a project robot account can act only within its own project, its permissions are chosen at creation, and it can have an expiration time. Giving CI push access and deployment targets pull-only access is an easy split to manage.
Robot account names carry a robot$ prefix by default, and that $ cost me some time. In 2023 I documented docker login returning unauthorized when integrating GitLab CI with Harbor. Interactive login worked, but inside the pipeline the $ was expanded as a variable. The fix at the time was to write $$ in .gitlab-ci.yml and pass the password with --password-stdin. According to the GitLab CI/CD variables documentation, variables defined in the UI do not expand $ references by default, so storing the account name as a CI/CD variable is another option worth considering.
Tagging Rules and Storage An image tag should trace back to source code. A common approach is to use version numbers for releases and the commit SHA for other builds. In 2020 I documented a small requirement: turning the Git tag v1.0.0 into the image tag 1.0.0 by dropping the first character with ${CI_COMMIT_TAG:1}. The rule is simple, but it should be decided early so every project follows the same convention.
Images only accumulate. Harbor offers several tools to manage them:
Tag retention: keep the tags you need by repository, count, or age, and remove the rest. The documentation recommends a dry run first because a run cannot be undone. Tag immutability: prevent release tags from being overwritten so a version number always points to the same image. Garbage collection: deleting tags or artifacts does not free space immediately. You need to run garbage collection to remove blobs that are no longer referenced. Long-term Operations: Upgrades, Backups, Signing Keys, and Log Limits Standing the system up is only the beginning. Most of the time goes into the years of maintenance that follow. These are the kinds of problems I recorded on my blog.
Upgrades: Required Stops Cannot Be Skipped In 2023 I documented upgrading GitLab from 14.9.3. A direct apt upgrade was blocked by the package’s preinstall check, which required moving to 14.10.x first. The fix was to step through versions with apt install gitlab-ce=<version>, restarting and checking services at each stop.
The lesson: the longer GitLab goes without an upgrade, the longer the path becomes. According to the GitLab upgrade paths documentation, required upgrade stops cannot be skipped; at each stop, upgrade to the latest patch release and let background migrations finish before continuing. GitLab also provides an Upgrade Path tool that calculates which stops apply. Small, regular upgrades are much safer than one large upgrade every few years.
Backups: Know What You Are Backing Up In 2023 I wrote a Bash script that uses the GitLab API to clone every project under an account, because a colleague needed all the repositories at once. A script like this is useful for migration or keeping a copy of the code, but it covers Git repositories only, not issues, merge requests, or CI/CD settings.
A complete GitLab backup still relies on the official backup process. According to the GitLab backup documentation, the backup task does not include configuration files. For Linux package installations, at minimum back up /etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json and /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb separately, and do not store them with the data backup. Without the secrets file, encrypted data in the database cannot be restored.
Package Signing Keys: They Will Expire Installing GitLab and Runner through apt means dealing with repository signing key rotation. I hit it twice:
In 2020, apt update reported NO_PUBKEY and the new GitLab GPG key had to be imported. In 2022, updating Runner on Ubuntu 18.04 failed with EXPKEYSIG because the key had expired, so it had to be downloaded and imported again. These issues do not take the service down immediately, but they make upgrades fail quietly. The apt-key command used in those posts is no longer recommended on newer Debian and Ubuntu releases, so follow GitLab’s current official instructions when handling this today.
Log Limits: 4 MB by Default In 2022 I ran into Runner reporting Job's log exceeded limit of 4194304 bytes. According to the Runner advanced configuration, output_limit under [[runners]] defaults to 4096 KB. Raising it keeps the job running, but the better fix is to find out why the log is so large, for example by turning off unnecessary verbose output.
What I Learned The cost of self-hosting comes later: installation happens once, while upgrades, backups, signing keys, and storage management recur every year and belong in a regular operations rhythm. Draw clear boundaries between stages: source, CI, image, and deploy each have their own components and permissions, which makes problems quick to locate. Design accounts and permissions for automation: robot accounts for CI and pull-only access for deployment are easier to manage and rotate than shared personal accounts. Write down the problems you hit: for every issue above, the fastest fix the next time was the record I left myself.
summary:
Since 2022, I have built and maintained self-hosted GitLab, GitLab Runner, Harbor registry, and CI/CD workflows as an Operator, connecting source code, container images, and deployment into one flow.
This is not a setup tutorial. Examples for .gitlab-ci.yml, Runner deployment, and multi-environment deployment are in the GitLab CI/CD Guide: Runner Setup, .gitlab-ci.yml, Harbor, and Deployments, and config.toml options and common variables are in GitLab Runner config.toml Configuration and Common CI/CD Variables. This post covers the other side: why you would run this stack yourself, how the components fit together, and where the time actually goes after a few years. Each problem mentioned below links to the record I wrote at the time on blog.clarence.tw.

Since 2022, part of my work has been bringing speech recognition technologies such as Kaldi and Whisper, together with GPU runtime, into real systems. That covers model inference, system deployment, and the performance maintenance that follows.
This is not a full case study of a specific project, and it does not include internal architecture, data, or performance numbers. Instead, it describes how I approach this kind of work: how I think about the differences between Kaldi and Whisper, why I stabilize the GPU runtime first, and what I check after deployment. Technical details follow the official documentation, and the troubleshooting lessons come from articles I have published on blog.clarence.tw (written in Chinese).
Where Speech AI Fits in a Product As I wrote in How I Work, LLM and Speech AI work is not just calling a model API. It has to connect with batch processing, local models, GPU runtime, and existing backend workflows.
Speech recognition is usually one stage of a larger flow. Typically, audio is captured, converted, and segmented before recognition; afterwards, the text is post-processed, stored, searched, or passed on to other services. So when I evaluate a Speech AI component, I look beyond the recognition result itself:
Is the input audio consistent in format and quality, and which layer owns preprocessing? Is recognition streaming or batch, and how are failures retried? How is the model output validated, and when does a person need to review it? Can this runtime be rebuilt on another machine? I learned early on that the same tool can behave very differently on different content. In 2019, when Amazon Transcribe added Simplified Chinese, I tried it and wrote up my impressions. A song gave poor results, while a conversation-heavy video worked much better. Whether you use a managed service or a self-hosted model, you need to judge it with audio close to your real use case.
Kaldi and Whisper: Characteristics and Trade-offs I use both Kaldi and Whisper in my work. I do not see one as a replacement for the other; they are tools built on very different design ideas.
Kaldi According to the Kaldi documentation, Kaldi is a speech recognition toolkit written in C++ and licensed under the Apache License v2.0, intended for speech recognition researchers. Its main characteristics include:
Finite state transducers (FSTs) at its core, built on OpenFst. The classic decoding graph is HCLG, composed from the HMM definitions, context dependency, lexicon, and grammar / language model. Recipes for many datasets, covering data preparation, training, and decoding. A library for online decoding, plus a batched CUDA decoding implementation under src/cudadecoder. From an operations perspective, Kaldi’s strength is its fine-grained components: the lexicon, language model, and acoustic model can each be adjusted. The cost is a long build process, a lot of required speech expertise, and an environment that breaks easily when compiler flags or dependencies differ.
Whisper According to openai/whisper, Whisper is a general-purpose speech recognition model based on a Transformer sequence-to-sequence architecture, trained on a large and diverse audio dataset. It supports multilingual transcription, translation into English, and language identification. The code and model weights are released under the MIT License.
Points that matter for deployment:
The model comes in tiny, base, small, medium, large, and turbo sizes. The official VRAM requirements range from roughly 1 GB to 10 GB, and speed varies widely, so model choice has to be made together with GPU capacity. It requires ffmpeg, and transcribe() processes the whole file with a 30-second sliding window. turbo is an optimized version of large-v3. It is fast but not trained for translation, so translation needs a multilingual model. The official model card warns that the model may produce text that was not spoken (hallucination), may repeat itself, and performs unevenly across languages, accents, and dialects. It also recommends against use in high-risk decision-making contexts. How I Choose Aspect Kaldi Whisper Design A pipeline of components (acoustic model, lexicon, language model, FST decoding) An end-to-end Transformer model Learning curve High; you need to understand recipes and the build process Low; install the package and start transcribing Adjustability Vocabulary, language model, and other components can be tuned separately Mostly through model size, decoding options, and pre/post-processing Multilingual Depends on training data and recipe Built-in multilingual transcription, translation into English, and language ID Watch out for Build environment, dependencies, model and graph versioning VRAM, long audio, hallucination, and repetition My rule is simple: compare with audio close to the real use case first, then weigh deployment and maintenance cost, rather than relying only on public benchmarks.
My Public Contribution to Kaldi My public contribution to Kaldi is a small fix: kaldi-asr/kaldi#4657, merged in December 2021. Opening Kaldi in Gitpod failed because the configuration referenced .gitpod.dockerfile, while the actual file was .gitpod.Dockerfile. The PR fixed the filename, removed a non-existent user and an unused path from the Dockerfile, and pinned the Intel MKL package version.
The change was small, but it reflects something I care about with tools like this: development and runtime environments should be reproducible by someone else.
Stabilize the GPU Runtime First: Driver, CUDA, Container Whether you use Kaldi or Whisper, once a GPU is involved there is a whole runtime stack beneath the model. I split it into layers and troubleshoot in this order:
Hardware and firmware settings: Is the GPU detected, and is Secure Boot enabled? Kernel and NVIDIA kernel module: Is the module built for the running kernel, and is it allowed to load? NVIDIA driver: Does nvidia-smi respond? CUDA and libraries: Are the CUDA runtime, cuDNN, and similar libraries compatible with the driver and framework? Container runtime: Can containers see the GPU? Application and model: PyTorch, the Kaldi build, and the model files themselves. Driver and CUDA Versions According to NVIDIA’s CUDA Compatibility documentation, the driver and CUDA toolkit can be upgraded on separate schedules. Starting with CUDA 11, minor version compatibility lets an application built within one major release family run on any driver at or above a minimum version (for example, 525 or newer for CUDA 12.x and 450 or newer for CUDA 11.x). Some features that need a newer driver are limited, and applications that compile device code to PTX for JIT are not covered.
In practice, this means deciding on the driver version first and then deciding which CUDA versions can run on top of it, instead of touching the driver every time a framework is upgraded.
Isolate CUDA and Frameworks with Containers The NVIDIA Container Toolkit requires the NVIDIA driver to be installed on the host. For Docker, after installing the packages, run:
BASH Copy sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker sudo systemctl restart docker nvidia-ctk modifies /etc/docker/daemon.json on the host, so this step belongs in configuration management. Then use the official sample workload to confirm containers can see the GPU:
BASH Copy sudo docker run --rm --runtime=nvidia --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi With this split, the host is mainly responsible for the driver and the container toolkit, while CUDA, cuDNN, and frameworks travel with the image. Different services can use different CUDA versions, and upgrades or rollbacks become a matter of switching images instead of repeatedly installing and removing packages on the host.
Problems I Have Documented These are GPU environment issues I have written about publicly (articles in Chinese). They did not necessarily happen in the same environment, but together they show why the runtime should be managed in layers:
Symptom Cause and fix Lesson nvidia-smi cannot communicate with the driver The driver module was not rebuilt after a kernel update; rebuild it for the new kernel with DKMS A kernel update is also a GPU environment change Driver fails to load under Secure Boot The locally built DKMS module was unsigned and rejected; switch to Ubuntu’s pre-signed linux-modules-nvidia-* packages You do not need to disable Secure Boot for the driver nvidia-smi reports No devices were found The packaged driver could not initialize the GPU; reinstall with NVIDIA’s official installer and resolve the kernel / GCC version mismatch When installation fails, read the kernel log and installer log first CUDA package dependencies cannot be installed The graphical session holds the driver; switch to multi-user.target before removing and reinstalling Driver updates need a maintenance window dpkg file overwrite error Different versions of NVIDIA packages try to overwrite the same file Keep driver package sources consistent on each machine NO_PUBKEY on a DGX system The NVIDIA CUDA repository changed its signing key; updating the key fixed it External repositories change too; read the update error first cuDNN verification sample fails to build The sample needs the extra FreeImage library Verification steps have dependencies of their own Two more posts, on CUDA Toolkit 11.7 installation methods (deb local, deb network, runfile) and selecting a GPU in darknet (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES versus framework-level settings), cover basics I still return to when planning a GPU environment.
Deployment and Performance Maintenance Checklist These are general checks; the details depend on the environment.
Before Deployment Record the full version set: OS, kernel, NVIDIA driver, CUDA, cuDNN, framework, model version, and image tag. Check the Secure Boot state (mokutil --sb-state) and decide whether to use pre-signed kernel modules or sign them yourself. Decide on an update policy for the kernel and driver so automatic updates do not change the GPU environment unnoticed. Estimate VRAM from model size and expected concurrency, then decide how many processes run on each GPU and how to assign them with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. After Deployment Host: confirm the module is loaded with lsmod | grep nvidia and that nvidia-smi responds. Container: run the sample workload to confirm containers can see the GPU. Application: run the full flow on a short, fixed test clip and confirm the output format and content make sense. Reboot and verify again so the driver and services recover on their own. Day-to-Day Monitoring Track GPU utilization and memory with commands such as nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv, or feed them into monitoring. Watch processing time and queue length to tell whether the bottleneck is GPU capacity, slow preprocessing, or I/O. Look for abnormal recognition output, such as heavy repetition or text that clearly is not in the audio. Risky Operations apt purge nvidia*, switching to multi-user.target, and removing or replacing kernel modules all interrupt GPU services. Schedule them in a maintenance window and confirm a recovery path first. nvidia-ctk runtime configure rewrites the Docker daemon configuration, so review it together with existing settings. Do not disable Secure Boot just for convenience; if it is truly necessary, assess the security impact first. What I Learned The model is only one layer. Whether Speech AI runs reliably over time depends heavily on how well the driver, kernel, CUDA, and container layers are managed. Keep the driver on the host and everything else in the image. With CUDA and frameworks in containers, upgrades and rollbacks become much simpler. Validate with your own use case. Kaldi and Whisper each have trade-offs. Public benchmarks are only a reference; the final comparison should use audio close to the real scenario. Write down the problems you hit. Every GPU issue I documented on my blog later became an item on my deployment checklists.

I do not treat Backend, AI, DevOps, Infrastructure, and Network as isolated areas. For a product that has to go online, be used, and remain maintainable, these layers eventually become one delivery chain.
Features need stable APIs. Services need reliable CI/CD. Long-running systems need monitoring, backup, network visibility, and security. When a product needs LLMs, Speech AI, or GPU runtime, model integration also has to be deployable, observable, and operable.
What I Work On Backend / API Backend is my core area. I work on API design, service integration, database access, existing system integration, and admin workflows. I use Node.js, Python, Go, PHP, C/C++, Shell Script, and Java depending on the existing architecture, maintainability, and runtime environment.
I care about whether an API is clear, whether data flow can be traced, whether errors can be diagnosed, and whether the system can still be maintained by the next person.
LLM / Speech AI Since 2022, I have worked on LLM and Speech AI in real product workflows. This is not just about calling a model API. It means connecting prompts, batch processing, local models, GPU runtime, OpenAI API, Ollama, Kaldi, Whisper, and existing backend workflows.
I prioritize control and operability: how inputs are prepared, how outputs are validated, how failures are retried, how cost is controlled, when to use local models or cloud APIs, and whether the runtime environment can be reproduced.
DevOps / CI/CD I maintain GitLab CI/CD, GitHub Actions, Jest tests, container image builds, deployment workflows, and release processes. The goal is to make releases repeatable and to know exactly which stage failed when something breaks.
For me, CI/CD is not only automated deployment. It is the connection between testing, builds, image registries, environment differences, rollback, and review workflows.
Cloud / On-prem Infrastructure I work across both cloud and on-prem environments. On the cloud side, that includes AWS CDK / IaC, AWS, GCP, Azure, and common service integrations. On-prem work includes Proxmox VE, Proxmox Backup Server, Harbor, GitLab, LDAP, LibreNMS, GPU servers, NAS, and backup planning.
This is also one reason I wrote AWS CDK 完全學習手冊: infrastructure should be describable, repeatable, and reviewable, instead of living only in one machine or one person’s memory.
Network / Security Operations I also work on enterprise network and security operations, including switches, firewalls, VLAN, VPN, SD-WAN, QoS, Wi-Fi, site-to-site backup, monitoring, and basic security controls.
Network is often underestimated. In real operations, many application issues eventually come back to DNS, routing, firewall rules, latency, Wi-Fi, certificates, proxy behavior, or missing monitoring visibility. Being able to trace from application behavior down to the network layer matters.
What This Site Should Communicate This site is not just a list of technologies. I want it to show the kind of engineering work I am good at:
Connecting Backend, AI, DevOps, and Infrastructure into deliverable systems. Writing applications while also handling deployment, runtime, monitoring, and network operations. Turning technical needs into implementations that can be operated, purchased, and handed over. Writing down lessons as articles, notes, or open-source projects. If I had to summarize it in one sentence: I am the kind of engineer who can help bring a product from code to stable production operation.
